newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia native title seen hitting farmers.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia native title seen hitting farmers.

text.p: Native title uncertainties had already begun to affect refinancing by Australian farmers and could affect future development, chief executive of the New South Wales Farmers' Association Peter Comensoli said Tuesday.
Agricultural output had not yet been affected, although there was a real risk that this could occur through stifled rural development, he told Reuters.

Widespread concern amongst farmers and miners has followed a ruling by Australia's High Court last month that a pastoral lease, for cattle or sheep farming, did not automatically extinguish aboriginal land claims on the same area.
The court found that the claim of the Wik Aboriginal group over 35,000 square km of land in Queensland may in some cases extinguish the rights of pastoral leaseholders in the area.

Comensoli was commenting after publicly calling on the Federal government to immediately introduce legislation to guarantee that pastoral leases extinguished native title, or to immediately prove to primary producers that they had an inalienable right to the land they held.

"Already we've had some situations in Queensland where pastoralists seeking to refinance have been asked questions that they hadn't previously, by banks, in relation to the security of their title," Comensoli said.
"There's a real risk that this uncertainty will stifle further development," he said.
Comensoli said it was expected that existing agricultural production in Australia would be maintained in the hope that the government would act responsibly.
"It's future development or the possibility of compensation for past development which is causing greatest grief," he said.
Comensoli told Reuters he was writing to Prime Minister John Howard to insist the government introduce legislation guaranteeing that pastoral leases extinguished native title.
"To say we're stepping up pressure on the government to legislate is an understatement," he said.
"I'm very dismayed by talk of fallback positions and other potential solutions."
Anything short of changing the statute would still rely on common law, and Australia's High Court already had determined that a pastoral lease did not extinguish native title, he said.
The Australian government had not given the association a straight answer on whether it would legislate, even though it had been directly asked, Comensoli said.

In a statement issued on Tuesday, NSW Farmers said that the Australian High Court, in its majority decision in the Wik case, had reopened what earlier had been resolved, that native title was extinguished by valid pastoral leases.

"Many pastoral leases are on land that passed to the control of farmers and graziers through agreement with earlier generations of aborigines. Now those agreements are being threatened by the existing generation," Comensoli said.
Many mining leases in Australia are also on former or existing pastoral leases, the most common form of land tenure in remote outback areas.
Some native title opponents estimate about 70 percent of Australia's land area could become subject to claims from Aborigines who number about two percent of the population.
